There are a number of factors that complicate reproduction of sound fidelity. First, sound is fundamentally different from imagery. Imagery is two-dimensional, and can be faithfully reproduced by projecting light through a lens to illuminate a phosphor-coated screen. Sound, on the other hand, is three-dimensional, and requires time to propagate through the air. In order to recreate the sound of a violin, for example, you don’t just need to replicate the vibrations of the strings, but also the reflections off the walls of the concert hall, the reverberations of the wood of the instrument, and so on.

Another complication is that human hearing is nonlinear. We perceive changes in loudness logarithmically, rather than linearly. This means that doubling the amplitude of a sound does not result in a doubling of perceived loudness. As a result, equalization curves are used to flatten the response of playback systems to mimic the way in which the human ear responds to sound.

## BackgroundEdit

A fisherman by trade, Haven Monroe's father was a well-respected member of the Gloucester fishing community. In 1912, the elder Monroe set out to sea on his boat, the Silver Dawn, but never returned. Several years later, while sailing alone, Haven's boat sprung a leak. Just as he was about to drown, Silas appeared in the nick of time and towed him to shore. Grateful for his life, Haven swore to repay the debt owed to Silas.

Aven, along with his father and several other Sironians, fought bravely against the invaders, but their numbers were no match for C'baoth's droid army. Carer participants expressed concern however, that lying could increase the person with dementia's confusion or negatively impact on their relationship with the person. Several alternative strategies to managing the person's anxiety, stress or agitation were identified. These ranged from: telling the truth, moving on the conversation, reframing the situation, distraction and "going with" the person. Carer participants did however confront or correct the person if they believed it was in their best interests. "Empathetic deception" captures their approach to "lying" or telling the truth: it was done in the person's best interest, in context of knowing what matters to the person and in a way that maintained the person's dignity. The person's capacity (loosely aligned to stage of dementia) was also considered and reflected in using different types of strategies e.g. it was more likely that carers would tell the truth in earlier stages and lie by omission or avoidance in the later stages. At the heart of carers' actions was the intention to benefit the person. They viewed an individualised approach, tailored to the person's needs and life history as critical, they questioned the benefit of hard and fast rules on "what to do" therefore. In context of the actions that formal carers should take, carers saw that therapeutic lying was appropriate when it benefited and respected the person's dignity. They viewed themselves as the representatives of the person with dementia's personhood in the later stages because they knew them, knew their life history and knew what mattered to them. Consequently they considered they had a role to play in preserving the person. They advised that in formal care settings a care plan should be agreed that reflected this knowledge.

Care planning is a process that involves assessing the needs of the person with dementia and their carer(s), formulating a plan of care and reviewing the plan on a regular basis. There is no universally accepted definition of care planning and this can vary between countries and health jurisdictions. In this study, care planning was defined as a collaborative process between the person with dementia, their carer(s) and health and social care professionals and encompasses assessment, planning, implementation and evaluation.́

## Methods

A Delphi study was undertaken to elicit the views of 10 experts in dementia care planning from the UK, New Zealand and Australia. The panel comprised academics, clinicians and policy makers with expertise in dementia care planning.

Four rounds of questionnaires were emailed to the panel over a period of 12 weeks. Responses were analysed using descriptive statistics and qualitative thematic analysis.

Thinkers such as Aristotle reasoned that the stars were part of the celestial sphere, and could not be seen during the day because the sun’s rays shone through them. It was a comforting thought, but not one that withstood scrutiny.

Another theory posited that the stars were in fact closer to Earth than the sun, and were obscured by the sun’s radiance. This was disproved by the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe, who in 1572 observed a new star in the constellation Cassiopeia. As the star, dubbed Nova Stella, was brighter than any of the stars in the Milky Way, it couldn’t be any closer to Earth than the sun.й that meant the sun was one of the stars.
